title: Hell
hook: traditions teach eternal separation; some hold that the lost cease to be; some hope all may be saved

segments.voice: Yesterday, heaven, and the small word at its center. Your line was with him. Who were you fully with, phone down? Day one thousand one hundred eight.

Near Jerusalem lies a valley. The Bible calls it the valley of the son of Hinnom, and Jeremiah says a terrible thing was done there: children burned in the fire, something God says he never commanded. When Jesus warns about hell in Matthew, the Greek word is Gehenna, and readers trace it to that valley's name. On that reading, a real place of horror became the name for final loss. It's a hard subject, and the churches hold it in more than one way. Today's word: hell.

Start with what Jesus says, because he says it seriously. In Matthew, after the sheep and the goats are separated: "these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal." And elsewhere he says to fear the one "which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." Catholic and Orthodox teaching, and the classic Protestant confessions, hold that hell is real and lasting: separation from God. Catholic teaching describes it as a person's own final choice to shut God out, not God's wish. Some Christians read that other line, destroy both soul and body, and hold that the lost finally cease to be. The fire, they say, is final, not endless. And some Christians, including some Orthodox writers, hope that God's love may in the end reach everyone. They lean on Paul, who says God "will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth." They hold it as a hope, not a promise. These readings disagree, and the disagreement matters. But they share two things. Each takes evil and its cost seriously. And each reads the same verse about God's heart. Peter writes that the Lord is "not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." On that verse, no one's loss is what God wants. An old hymn puts it in a line: "There's a wideness in God's mercy."

Here's the practice: hold everyone. Breathe slowly, and start close: the people in your home, the people you'll see today. Then widen: your street, your city, people you'll never meet. Then the hard ones: someone who hurt you, someone whose choices you can't understand at all. Don't argue with yourself about whether they deserve it. If you pray, you can bring them before God, the way Paul asks prayers to be made for all. If you don't, just wish each one well, as widely as you can reach. The bell holds the time.
Hell. In the Gospels, Gehenna: a word readers trace to a valley's name, used for final loss. Churches read it as lasting separation, as an end, or alongside a hope that all be saved.
Your line: his mercy is wide. Today, give one person more mercy than they've earned from you. Day one thousand one hundred eight.

howItsDone: Christians meet the teaching on hell in the Gospels' warnings and in the creeds' judgment of the living and the dead; Catholic and Orthodox teaching and the classic Protestant confessions hold it as real and lasting separation from God, while some Christians hold other views.

notes: Gehenna as the Greek form of the Hebrew name of the valley of Hinnom: standard lexicon fact, but an etymology; confirm. Jeremiah 7:31 paraphrased (children burned; 'which I commanded them not').

Three views (eternal separation; conditional immortality/annihilationism; hopeful universalism) named without ranking; 'including some Orthodox writers' for the hope that all be saved is uncounted; confirm wording.
Catholic teaching on hell as definitive self-exclusion (Catechism 1033) paraphrased; confirm.
The hymn line is from Frederick W. Faber's 19th-century hymn (public domain); no date given in the script.
Index carry 'his mercy is wide' kept exactly.

Editor: the Gehenna-Hinnom link is an etymology the cited texts don't state, so it is now attributed to 'readers' throughout (hook, word, match, myth, original, trapdoor); 'the word he uses in the Gospels' narrowed to Matthew (Luke 16 uses Hades); unsupported 'outside Jerusalem' dropped; garbled 'whatever happens at the end is not what God wants' rewritten as 'no one's loss is what God wants'.
Auditor: no changes. Matthew 25:46, 10:28, 1 Tim 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9 checked against the KJV; Faber line correct; three views named without ranking.
